overview: This 800 to 1279 atlas entry groups many communities across western and central Mexico and Oaxaca. Its broad outline is not one state, one language or all of Mesoamerica. Cities traded, competed and changed under different rulers. The Maya, Nahua, Zapotec, Mixtec and other peoples retain their distinct histories; named states have separate cards.

periods.title: Cities at the end of the Classic era
periods.summary: Cantona’s peak extended approximately from 600 to 900, beginning well before this map interval. Different centres followed different histories.

periods.title: Household industries and changing centres
periods.summary: Cholula’s Early Postclassic households made textiles and used distinctive pottery while the city’s ceremonial life continued.

periods.title: Later kingdoms and new arrangements
periods.summary: Yagul’s Late Postclassic palace belongs to a 1200 to 1521 phase, extending far beyond this atlas endpoint.

items.text: The sampled outlines include Cantona and Yagul, but exclude Tula and Cacaxtla. Xochicalco appears inside the 800 outline and outside later ones; Cholula changes in the opposite direction. These are coarse map decisions, not evidence that the cities shared a government. The Maya heartland lies largely beyond this particular record.

Long-distance exchange helped carry objects and visual styles between cities. That made the region connected without making it politically uniform. The Met’s regional survey distinguishes central Mexican city-states, Gulf Coast centres and Oaxaca kingdoms rather than giving them one capital. A familiar-looking vessel could cross a border more easily than a king’s authority.

At Cantona in Puebla, homes occupied compounds enclosed by walls. Patio 2 contained fourteen architectural structures and two entrances, with a passage to a neighbouring compound. Archaeologists interpret the connection as evidence that the two units were closely related. It does not tell us precisely which relatives, workers or neighbours lived there.

Cantona’s Calzada 1 runs for more than 500 metres through the lower residential area, passing thirty-four patios or housing units and connecting with other routes. This was infrastructure for moving around a real city. The archaeological map contains streets and neighbourhood connections as well as pyramids.

Cantona’s excavated kitchen equipment includes grinding stones, large jars for grain and water, and smaller cooking vessels. Some pots were shaped like feet and preserve traces of food preparation. The museum calls them patojos: footwear-shaped pottery belonged in the kitchen, not on somebody’s feet.

Other Cantona tools were used to prepare ixtle plant fibre. This puts thread-making and other fibre work beside stoneworking in the city’s economy. Animal bones, musical instruments and ornaments also survive. Everyday life required different kinds of skilled work, even though obsidian attracts much of the attention.

A 2010 study tested seventy-nine obsidian samples using neutron activation analysis. The investigators compared material from Cantona workshops and nearby settlements, identifying the importance of Oyameles-Zaragoza obsidian. Chemical composition helps trace a tool’s material back toward its source, adding a second kind of evidence to its shape.

The Cantona museum was built around finds from repeated archaeological seasons. Its account distinguishes these from an earlier, privately excavated collection that lacked a proper inventory. Knowing where a pot or tool came from matters: an object beside a hearth tells a different story from one placed in an offering.

At Xochicalco in Morelos, a cistern received rainwater through underground conduits from higher ground. Storing runoff helped supply a hilltop settlement. This is direct evidence of water engineering; it does not establish that every home had running water or a sewage connection.

Nearby stood a square steam bath with a place for heating stones using firewood. INAH estimates room for about fifteen people and interprets it as preparation for ritual ballgames. Bathing here joined bodily care and ceremony. This particular structure does not supply evidence for a universal medical treatment.

Masonry tools and plumb bobs were found in Xochicalco’s so-called Temple of the Architects. They bring the builders into view alongside the finished monuments. Making straight walls involved practical knowledge and instruments; the modern building name does not prove that this was an ancient school.

A short authentic sign reading comes from Xochicalco’s Two-Glyph Stela: “Year 10 Reed; day 9 Reptile Eye.” These are modern English labels for its carved calendar signs, not reconstructed spoken words. The monument belongs to the Epiclassic city, approximately 650 to 900. Its original is in the site museum; the plaza displays a replica.

Another Xochicalco slab shows a woman carried along a path marked with footprints toward a seated man. Silvia Garza Tarazona interprets the scene as a marriage alliance between communities, with calendrical names read as 3 Monkey and 2 Movement. The museum dates the object broadly to 200 to 900 CE; the proposed reading is not a record of every family’s marriage customs.

At Cholula’s Early Postclassic UA-1 household, archaeological analysis identifies intensive spinning and waterfowl hunting. McCafferty suggests feathers may have been gathered for textiles. The spinning and hunting evidence supports household industry; using those feathers in cloth remains an interpretation. Work at home could connect several resources and skills.

Cholula had abundant polychrome pottery by about 900. Some early designs resemble Gulf Coast and Maya imagery. McCafferty argues that Cholula’s ceremonial activity continued through major cultural change rather than simply ending when Teotihuacan declined. Shared styles therefore raise questions about contact and local choices, not just conquest.

Yagul in Oaxaca offers a later comparison. Its Palace of Six Patios is dated broadly to 1200 to 1521, mostly beyond this card’s span. INAH distinguishes public and private courts and tentatively associates the central pair with the ruler’s family. Government and elite household life occupied connected, differently accessible spaces.

A small pear-shaped bell in the Met illustrates western or central Mexican metalworking. It is dated broadly to the eleventh through sixteenth centuries, so it cannot be assigned specifically to this map’s years. Its suspension loop and hollow body show how a wearable or hanging object could also make sound.

The bell was made by lost-wax casting, including the ridged decoration that resembles fine wirework. Its internal clapper is missing. The curator notes that a clapper could have been metal, stone or pottery; striking the bell against another object could also make it ring. Metal craft involved sound as well as appearance.

Cantona did not remain a thriving city until 1279 simply because the umbrella outline continues. Excavation director Ángel García Cook placed its abandonment between about 900 and 1050. Cholula followed another path of continuing activity and later political change. There was no single event that ended all these centres together.

Living Indigenous languages are part of the region’s present. INALI’s language atlas documents communities and speakers in the twenty-first century, including audio and contemporary geographic information. Those communities have their own names and histories. A medieval umbrella label cannot replace them or describe their modern borders.

ending.text: The atlas ends this label in 1279, not with one shared conquest. Particular cities declined, changed rulers or continued; later states transformed the region again. Indigenous communities and languages remain living parts of Mexico. Their continuity should not be confused with uninterrupted survival of every earlier government.
